channel.title: HAT MI Daily - Macro and Industries
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: The US ISM non-manufacturing index fell to 54.5 in October from 54.9, with new orders at 55.9, a four-month low, and unfilled orders at their highest level since 2022, Cnyes reports.
item.description:
Cnyes, citing the Institute for Supply Management (ISM), reports that the US non-manufacturing index declined from 54.9 to 54.5 in October. The business activity index dropped from 56.5 to 53.8 and the new orders index from 59.8 to 55.9, a four-month low, while the unfilled orders index rose to its highest level since 2022 and the employment index rose from 50.1 to 51.4. The row adds that the US services Purchasing Managers' Index declined from 58.8 to 56.1 and the composite PMI from 58.4 to 55.9, without naming the compiler. The row does not give the sector breakdown, the readings for earlier months or the reasons for the changes.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports survey indices for the non-manufacturing sector, which it does not split into construction or other industries. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, an index still well above 50 with lower business activity and lower new orders describes non-manufacturing activity that continues to grow at a slower pace. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, non-manufacturing activity bears on construction and manufacturing demand only indirectly; the row gives no sector figures. Points that may be worth considering include the November reading, the ISM manufacturing index and US construction spending data.

Cnyes

item.title: Brazil's central bank kept its Selic rate at 13.75% on 4 November in a unanimous vote, ending a run of cuts that began in March, after the currency and stock market fell following Lula's re-election, MarketScreener reports.
item.description:
MarketScreener reports that Brazil's central bank ended a run of interest rate cuts that began in March and held borrowing costs, with its rate-setting committee Copom voting unanimously to keep the Selic rate at 13.75% on 4 November 2026. It says policymakers pledged to keep monetary policy adequately restrictive to return inflation to target, and that the decision follows a sharp fall in the value of the currency and of the stock market after President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's win over senator Flávio Bolsonaro in the runoff on 25 October. The row does not give inflation figures or forecasts, the size of the cuts since March, the exchange rate level or the date of the next meeting.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports one decision from one outlet. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a pause after a run of cuts keeps borrowing costs high for Brazilian companies and households for longer than a continued run of cuts would. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, construction and manufacturing demand in Brazil depends partly on financing costs, so a rate that stays high can weigh on projects financed with credit; the row gives no demand data. Points that may be worth considering include Brazilian inflation data, the exchange rate and the committee's next decision.

MarketScreener

item.title: The Mission Possible Partnership's tracker records a record 36 commercial-scale industrial decarbonisation projects reaching final investment decision in 12 months, 23 in China, which holds 49% of clean-industry plants operating or under construction.
item.description:
The Standard reports that the Mission Possible Partnership's Global Project Tracker shows that China secured USD 45 billion in clean-industry investment in 2026 and accounts for 49% of all clean industrial plants currently operating or under construction. In the past 12 months a record 36 commercial-scale industrial decarbonisation projects reached final investment decision, 23 of them in China, and the leading sectors were sustainable aviation fuel, methanol and clean ammonia. Lianhe Zaobao, citing the same tracking data, adds that 189 such projects have been financed or built globally, 93 of them in China, and that another 838 have been announced or are in development. The rows do not give the investment total outside China, the definition of a clean-industry plant, the capacity of the projects or the sectors beyond those named.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report counts and an investment figure from one tracker, not output or prices. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a concentration of final investment decisions in China describes where new low-carbon capacity is being financed, which can shape where such products are produced and at what cost. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, methanol and ammonia are base chemicals that feed other chemical products, so projects for low-carbon versions could change where such feedstocks are made and their cost; the rows give no volumes or prices. Points that may be worth considering include the tracker's next update, the capacity of the methanol and ammonia projects and announcements by European producers.

The Standard | Lianhe Zaobao

item.title: China and Canada agreed on 3 November to extend their mutual tariff exemptions to the end of 2028, covering Canadian canola meal, peas, lobsters and crabs and certain Chinese steel and aluminium products, Commercial Times and BNN Bloomberg report.
item.description:
Commercial Times reports that the first ministerial meeting of the 29th China-Canada Joint Economic and Trade Committee was co-chaired in Beijing on 3 November by Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao and Canadian International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu, and that both countries agreed to extend mutual tariff exemption measures until the end of 2028. It says the agreement was finalised by Prime Minister Mark Carney and President Xi Jinping during Carney's visit to China in January 2026, that Canadian exports of canola meal, peas, lobsters and crabs to China continue at low tariff rates for two more years and that Canada extends the exemption for Chinese steel and aluminium products by two years. BNN Bloomberg, citing Sidhu, reports that the January agreement was due to expire at the end of 2026, that Canada agreed to allow in certain Chinese steel and aluminum products in return for Chinese market access for imports from Canada, and that Ottawa aims to increase exports to China by 50% by 2030. The rows do not give tariff rates, quotas or volumes for steel and aluminium or any US reaction.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report an extension of existing arrangements, not new tariff cuts. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, extending the exemption for Chinese steel and aluminium products keeps a route for those metals into the Canadian market that would otherwise lapse at the end of 2026. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, steel and aluminium are bonded and coated in construction and vehicles, so the supply of these metals could affect the cost of products made in Canada; the rows give no volumes or prices. Points that may be worth considering include the product list and quotas for steel and aluminium, reactions of Canadian steel producers and any effect on Canada's talks with the United States.

Commercial Times | BNN Bloomberg

item.title: Thailand's finance minister says a 35% excise tax on fully built imported electric vehicles takes effect on 1 January 2027 and will be explained to foreign carmakers with Thai plants, including Japanese ones, The Nation reports.
item.description:
The Nation reports that Thailand's Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas said the government will explain the details of the 35% excise tax on fully built imported electric vehicles to foreign carmakers that have invested in manufacturing bases in Thailand. The briefings will include Japanese manufacturers during an investment roadshow in Japan. The report gives 1 January 2027 as the effective date and says the measure aims to ensure fair competition for investors that establish manufacturing bases and employ Thai workers. The row does not give the previous tax rate, the origin or volume of the vehicles affected, any exemptions, the date of the roadshow or carmakers' reactions.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports one tax measure and a plan to brief carmakers, not its effect on trade or production. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a 35% excise tax on fully built imported vehicles raises their price against electric vehicles assembled in Thailand and favours local assembly. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, electric vehicles assembled locally use bonding, sealing and coating materials, so a shift from imports to local assembly of electric vehicles could raise demand for such materials in Thailand; the row gives no volumes or materials. Points that may be worth considering include the origin of the vehicles the tax covers, investment announcements by carmakers in Thailand and import data after 1 January.

The Nation

item.title: IG Metall demands 5% more pay over 12 months and job and site guarantees in the German metal and electrical industry, employers offered a one-time payment and a 1.3% rise in July 2028, and warning strikes continue, Süddeutsche Zeitung reports.
item.description:
Süddeutsche Zeitung reports that IG Metall plans further negotiations during the warning strikes in the collective bargaining dispute in the German metal and electrical industry. For the Mitte bargaining area, which covers Hesse, Rhineland-Palatinate and Saarland, talks are to continue in Frankfurt on Friday. IG Metall demands 5% more money over a 12-month period and the safeguarding of jobs and locations. In the second round of negotiations, which the row does not tie to a single bargaining area, employers presented an offer of a one-time payment next year and a staggered increase of 1.3% in July 2028, which the row describes as below the inflation rate and justifies with the difficult economic situation and the high cost burdens for industry in Germany. The row does not give the number of employees covered, the dates or scale of the warning strikes, the size of the one-time payment, the inflation rate it compares with or the employers' association's statement.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports negotiating positions and the warning strikes, of which only the Friday round is tied to one bargaining area, not an agreement. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a 5% demand over 12 months and an offer of a one-time payment of unstated size and a 1.3% rise in July 2028 cannot be compared exactly from the row, which describes the offer as below the inflation rate, and warning strikes are a step in a dispute that can end in a settlement later. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, the metal and electrical industry includes machinery, vehicle and electrical component makers that buy bonding, sealing and coating materials, so a long dispute could affect their output and a settlement would set their labour costs; the row names no companies or products. Points that may be worth considering include the outcome of Friday's round in Frankfurt, the scale of further warning strikes and settlement terms in other bargaining areas.

Süddeutsche Zeitung

item.title: Democrats win control of both houses of Congress in the US midterms, outlets report, with seat counts differing between sources, while experts quoted say tariffs under existing laws are unlikely to change.
item.description:
Handelsblatt reports that voters handed full control of Congress to the Democrats, who won Senate seats in Kansas, Texas, Ohio and Michigan, and Nikkei Asian Review reports that the Associated Press called the House for the Democrats after the party passed 218 seats and that voters were unhappy with Republican policy on inflation, tariffs, AI data centres and the Iran war. Seat counts differ: Fortune gives counts of 54–44 in the Senate and 228–129 in the House on the morning of 4 November, while the projections differ: Global Times, citing the CNBC Election Desk, gives the Democrats at least 245 House and at least 54 Senate seats, Bjd.com.cn, citing Decision Desk HQ, gives them 52 of 100 Senate seats, and MarketScreener, citing Reuters, gives them at least 235 House seats. Il Sole 24 Ore reports Trump saying he was "absolutely willing to accept those results" and would cooperate with the Democrats while posting a "Veto" cap on Truth Social, and Handelsblatt reports that he said he would not permanently use his veto rights on legislation. The Economic Times reports Trump saying Vance's charge that the Iran war caused the loss was "largely true". MarketScreener quotes trade experts who say the Democrats can scrutinise trade policy and use control of agency funding to seek concessions but are largely unable to override a veto on votes to overturn tariffs, and the Globe and Mail cites experts who say tariffs under the 1962 and 1974 trade laws are on sound legal footing and will not be amended without a 60-seat Senate majority, while duties under Section 338 of the 1930 trade law may fail in court. Handelsblatt reports the Dow Jones up 3% to 53,356 points and the S&P 500 up 1.6%, The Guardian reports the US dollar at a one-month low, and The Straits Times reports data centre shares falling on fears of tighter AI regulation. The rows do not give final seat counts, the date the new Congress sits or a White House statement on tariffs.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report a result, counts that differ between outlets and expert commentary on tariffs. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a Congress controlled by the opposition can hold hearings, use its budget powers and slow legislation, while the experts quoted describe the tariff statutes as out of reach of a repeal that survives a veto, so the rows point to continued tariffs with more scrutiny. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, US tariffs on imports and on trading partners such as Canada affect the cost of raw materials and of inputs for construction and manufacturing; the rows give no tariff rates or product lists. Points that may be worth considering include final seat counts, House hearings or votes on tariff actions and tariff announcements by the White House after the election.

Handelsblatt | Nikkei Asian Review | Fortune | Global Times | Bjd.com.cn | Il Sole 24 Ore | Handelsblatt | The Economic Times | MarketScreener | The Globe and Mail | Handelsblatt | The Guardian | The Straits Times

item.title: German mechanical and plant engineers received 14% more orders in September than a year earlier, price-adjusted, with orders from Germany up 22% and from abroad up 11%, VDMA data cited by Handelsblatt show.
item.description:
Handelsblatt, citing the VDMA, reports that German mechanical and plant engineers received 14% more orders in September 2026 than in September 2025, adjusted for price effects: orders from Germany rose 22% year on year and orders from abroad 11%. For the first nine months of 2026, orders rose 5%, without a statement on whether this figure is price-adjusted. The row also says that new business in the euro zone was weak, with a 5% decline, that domestic business stagnated and that 13% more orders came from foreign countries outside the euro zone, without stating the period for these three figures. The VDMA expects production to decline for the fourth year in a row in 2026. The row does not give the order volume, the customer industries behind the rise, the reason for the strong domestic orders or the size of the expected production decline.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports order intake, not production or sales. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, the row gives a price-adjusted 14% rise for September and a 5% rise for nine months without saying whether the second figure is price-adjusted or what base it uses, so the two cannot be compared exactly, and the expected fourth annual fall in production shows that the VDMA does not read the orders as a turn. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, machinery and plant makers buy bonding, sealing and coating materials for assembly and for their machines' components, and orders reach production with a delay; the row names no materials. Points that may be worth considering include the VDMA's October orders, the customer industries behind the domestic rise and German machinery production data.

Handelsblatt

item.title: The KBA reports 94,086 purely electric cars newly registered in Germany in October, up 80% year on year and 37% of the market, in a total of 254,492 registrations, up 1.7%, Frankfurter Rundschau writes.
item.description:
Frankfurter Rundschau, citing the Federal Motor Transport Authority (KBA), reports that 94,086 purely electric passenger cars were newly registered in Germany in October 2026, up 80% on the same month of the previous year, taking their market share to 37%. Plug-in hybrids numbered 28,499, down 7.9%, with a share of 11.2%, and 48.2% of all newly registered passenger cars had an externally rechargeable electric drive. Total new registrations were 254,492, up 1.7% on the same month of the previous year, a market development the row describes as significantly weaker without giving a comparison for that description. In the first ten months of 2026, 2.48 million passenger cars were newly registered, up 4.9% on the year. The row does not give registrations by brand, the electric-car figure for October 2025, vehicle production or the reasons for the rise.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports registrations in Germany, not vehicle production, and one outlet's account of KBA data. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, an 80% rise in electric registrations within a market that grew 1.7% describes a change in the mix of drive types. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, electric vehicles use bonding, sealing and coating materials in their battery systems and lightweight structures as well as in conventional assembly, so a mix shift could change which materials are specified; the row gives no figures for materials. Points that may be worth considering include the November registration data, registrations by manufacturer and German vehicle production data.

Frankfurter Rundschau

item.title: Brent fell more than 8% on 4 November to about USD 94 to 95 on investor bets that the Democratic midterm win could bring the end of the Iran war closer, while industry executives say prices may stay elevated.
item.description:
Kompas.com reports that WTI closed at USD 88.12 a barrel, down 8.3%, and Brent fell 8.7% to USD 94.62, after Vice President JD Vance said the war against Iran caused the Republican defeat in the midterm elections, and that investors believe the result could encourage President Trump to seek a deal to end the conflict. Nihon Keizai Shimbun gives the same WTI close, USD 7.97 below the previous day and the third consecutive daily fall, with an intraday low of USD 87.13, the lowest in about a month, and says there is a view that the result will pressure the administration to end the conflict. Business Standard reports Brent futures down 10% to a session low of USD 93.22, the lowest in two months, and Yahoo reports a fall of up to 10% for Brent to USD 93, the first time since 7 October that Brent was below USD 100. The Economic Times reports on 5 November that both benchmarks fell by more than 8% in the previous session to settle at their lowest since 31 August, that oil fell for a fourth day, and that two sources close to Gulf government circles say a weakened Trump facing a Democratic Congress able to constrain his military options has a greater incentive to seek a deal. Commercial Times reports Brent at USD 93.65 in Asian morning trade on 5 November, down 1.03%, and Arab News reports Brent at USD 104.42 early on 4 November. A further Economic Times report quotes industry executives who say prices may remain elevated because a weakened Trump could intensify military operations or find it harder to end the war; it gives WTI down 7.8% at USD 88.54, which differs from the WTI figures above. The rows do not give an official US or Iranian statement on talks, shipping data for the Strait of Hormuz or the times of most of the quotes.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report price moves and expectations about a deal, not a change in oil flows. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, crude and its products set the cost of many raw materials with a lag, and a fall driven by expectations rather than by supply can reverse if the expectations fade, as the executives' view in the rows allows. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, lower oil prices could ease the cost of resins, solvents and freight with a delay, while the rows give no prices for these. Points that may be worth considering include an official US or Iranian statement on talks, Brent over the next trading days and shipping data for the Strait of Hormuz.
